<reason>Side A (CON) controlled the scope clash from opening to close: every PRO harm (inheritance, grandchildren, future generations) lives on the germline side of a line PRO admitted is already drawn, while the motion criminalizes somatic adult choice. PRO's fallback—enforcement collapse, because edits can't be externally verified—was his best material (especially the off-target gonadal exposure point), but A landed two counters B never fully absorbed: unverifiability cuts both ways (a ban polices only the honest and pushes the rest offshore), and the proves-too-much point that therapeutic somatic gene therapy uses the same invisible edits in the same clinics, which B left unanswered through Rebuttal 2 and Closing. A answered pressure questions directly with A1/A2 structure and adapted each round; B's answers, while coherent, increasingly reframed the motion from 'name a victim of the somatic edit' to 'the industry will drift,' a widening A exploited. B's clipped opening is a minor execution cost. B's ceiling/multiplex-editting answer to A's Q2 was genuinely good, but not enough to offset the unanswered gene-therapy parallel and the burden gap on the case the proposition actually bans.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was A's Q1 ('name the harm of a somatic, non-heritable edit') against B's enforcement-collapse answer: B argued regulators cannot verify which line was crossed, and A's reply that invisibility refutes the ban itself—since unverifiable edits are also undetectable under prohibition, which merely relocates them to recordless clinics—combined with the unanswered point that the same logic would ban somatic gene therapy, left B's last line of victory visibly cracked.</best_rebuttal>
